1. When the ruling faculty is in keeping with nature, it meets whatever happens in such a way that it always adapts itself easily to what is possible and to what is put before it. For it does not demand any fixed material to work on. It moves toward its purpose, though only on certain conditions; and it turns whatever stands in its way into material for itself. It is like a fire that takes hold of whatever falls into it. A small flame would have been put out by these things; but when the fire is strong, it quickly makes whatever is heaped on it its own, burns it up, and rises higher by means of that very material.
2. Let nothing you do be done without a purpose, or in any way other than by the principles that bring an art to perfection.

3. People look for places to get away to: houses in the country, the seashore, the mountains. And you too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But this is entirely the mark of the most ordinary sort of person, since it is in your power, whenever you choose, to withdraw into yourself. For there is nowhere a person can withdraw to with more quiet or more freedom from trouble than into his own soul—especially if he has thoughts within him such that, by looking into them, he is at once perfectly calm. And I say that calm is nothing other than a mind in good order. So give yourself this retreat constantly, and renew yourself. Let your principles be brief and basic, so that as soon as you turn to them they will be enough to wash the soul completely clean, and to send you back free of all resentment toward the things you are returning to. For what is it you resent? The badness of people? Call to mind this conclusion: that rational beings exist for one another; that bearing with others is part of justice; and that people do wrong against their will. And think how many people, after hostility, suspicion, hatred and fighting, have been laid out dead and turned to ashes. And be quiet at last. But perhaps you are discontented with what the universe has allotted you. Then call to mind this alternative: either there is providence, or there are only atoms—things thrown together by chance. Or remember the arguments that have proved that the world is a kind of community of citizens. And be quiet at last. But perhaps the things of the body will still take hold of you. Then consider further that the mind, once it has drawn itself apart and recognized its own power, does not mix with the breath, whether the breath moves gently or roughly. And think, too, of everything you have heard about pain and pleasure and have agreed to. And be quiet at last. But perhaps the craving for what is called fame will torment you. Then see how quickly everything is forgotten. Look at the chaos of endless time on either side of the present; at how empty applause is; at how changeable and lacking in judgment are those who make a show of praising; and at how narrow the space is within which praise is confined. And be quiet at last. For the whole earth is a point, and your home is a tiny corner of it; and how few people live there, and what sort of people they are who will praise you! What remains, then, is this: remember to withdraw into this little territory of your own. Above all, do not pull yourself this way and that, or strain yourself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. And among the things closest to hand, which you will turn to, let there be these two. The first is that things do not touch the soul: they stand outside it and do not move, and our disturbances come only from the opinion within. The second is that all these things you see will change in a moment and will no longer be; and keep constantly in mind how many such changes you have already seen for yourself. The universe is change; life is opinion.

4. If the power of thought is common to us all, then reason too, which makes us rational beings, is common to us all. If so, then the reason that tells us what to do and what not to do is also common. If so, there is also a common law. If so, we are fellow citizens. If so, we are members of some community of citizens. If so, the world is in a way a state. For what other shared community could anyone say the whole human race belongs to? And it is from there, from this shared community, that we get our very power of thought, our power of reasoning and our capacity for law—or where else do they come from? For just as the earthy part of me is a portion given to me from some earth, and the watery part from another element, and the hot and fiery part from some source of its own (for nothing comes out of nothing, just as nothing returns into nothing), so the thinking part too comes from some source.

5. Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature: a coming together of the same elements, and a coming apart into the same elements. And it is not at all something anyone should be ashamed of. For it is not against the nature of a rational being, and not against the reason by which we are made.

6. It is natural that people like this should act like this; it is a matter of necessity. Anyone who will not have it so will not allow the fig tree to have its juice. But above all remember this: in a very short time both you and he will be dead, and soon not even your names will be left behind.
7. Take away your opinion, and the complaint "I have been harmed" is taken away. Take away the complaint "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
8. What does not make a person worse than he was does not make his life worse either, and does not harm him, from outside or from within.
9. The nature of what is useful to all has been compelled to do this.

10. Consider that everything that happens, happens justly; if you watch carefully, you will find that it is so. I do not mean only that things follow one another in an unbroken order. I mean that they happen justly, as if done by someone who gives each thing what it is worth. So go on watching, as you have begun. And whatever you do, do it together with this: being good, in the true sense in which a person is understood to be good. Keep to this in every action.
11. Do not take the view of things that the person who wrongs you takes, or the view he wants you to take. Look at them as they truly are.

12. A person should always have these two rules ready. The first is to do only what the reason of the ruling and law-giving faculty suggests for the good of human beings. The second is to change your opinion, if someone is at hand to set you right and move you away from some opinion. But this change of opinion must come only from being persuaded of something, such as that it is just or for the common good, or the like—not because it seems pleasant or brings you a good name.
13. Do you have reason? I do.—Then why do you not use it? For if it is doing its own work, what else do you want?
14. You have existed as a part. You will vanish into what produced you; or rather, you will be taken back by change into its generative principle—the seed of reason from which things grow.
15. Many grains of frankincense on the same altar: one falls sooner, another later; but it makes no difference.
16. Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people who now think you a beast and an ape—if you go back to your principles and to your reverence for reason.
17. Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.

18. How much trouble a person spares himself when he does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only at what he does himself, so that it may be just and pure! Or, as Agathon says, do not look around at the corrupt ways of others, but run straight along the line without swerving from it.

19. Someone who has a burning desire for fame after death does not consider that every one of those who remember him will very soon die too; and then, in turn, those who come after them; until the whole memory of him has been snuffed out, as it is passed along through people who foolishly admire and then perish. But suppose that those who will remember you were even immortal, and that the memory would be immortal: what is that to you? And I do not mean, what is it to the dead? I mean, what is it to the living? What is praise, except perhaps insofar as it has some practical use? For now you are rejecting nature's gift at the wrong time, and clinging to something else....

20. Everything that is beautiful in any way is beautiful in itself, and its beauty ends there, in itself; praise is no part of it. So a thing is made neither worse nor better by being praised. I say this also of the things that ordinary people call beautiful, such as material objects and works of art. What is truly beautiful needs nothing further—no more than law does, no more than truth, no more than kindness or modesty. Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or spoiled because it is blamed? Is an emerald made worse than it was if it is not praised? Or gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a shrub?

21. If souls go on existing, how does the air hold them all from eternity?—But how does the earth hold the bodies of those who have been buried for so many ages? Here on earth, after these bodies have lasted for a certain time, whatever it may be, they change and break up, and so make room for other dead bodies. In the same way, the souls that move into the air last for some time, and then they are changed and spread out, and take on a fiery nature as they are taken back into the generative intelligence of the universe. In this way they make room for the new souls that come to live there. This is the answer one might give on the assumption that souls go on existing. But we must think not only of the number of bodies that are buried in this way, but also of the number of animals that are eaten every day by us and by other animals. What a number is consumed, and so in a way buried in the bodies of those who feed on them! And yet the earth holds them, because these bodies are changed into blood and transformed into air or fire. How is the truth of this matter to be investigated? By dividing things into what is material and what is the cause that gives them form.
22. Do not be spun around. In every impulse, hold to what is just; and with every impression, keep hold of your power to grasp and understand it.

23. Everything that is in harmony with you, O Universe, is in harmony with me. Nothing that comes at the right time for you is too early or too late for me. Everything your seasons bring, O Nature, is fruit to me. From you are all things, in you are all things, to you all things return. The poet says, "Dear city of Cecrops"; and will you not say, "Dear city of Zeus"?

24. "Do few things," says the philosopher, "if you want to be calm." But consider whether it would not be better to say: Do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a being made by nature for community requires, and in the way it requires. For this brings not only the calm that comes from doing things well, but also the calm that comes from doing few things. Most of what we say and do is unnecessary; if a person cuts it away, he will have more leisure and less unease. So on every occasion a person should ask himself: Is this one of the unnecessary things? And he should cut away not only unnecessary acts but also unnecessary thoughts; for then unnecessary acts will not follow after them.
25. Try how the life of the good person suits you: the life of someone who is content with his share of the whole, and content with his own just acts and kindly disposition.

26. Have you seen those things? Now look at these too. Do not trouble yourself. Make yourself wholly simple. Is someone doing wrong? It is himself he wrongs. Has something happened to you? Very well. Everything that happens was allotted to you and spun out for you from the universe from the beginning. In a word: your life is short. You must make good use of the present, with the help of reason and justice. Be sober even when you relax.

27. Either the universe is well ordered, or it is a chaos thrown together—but even so, a universe. But can there be some order in you, and disorder in the whole? And that, too, when all things are so distinct from one another, and so spread through everything, and so in sympathy with one another?
28. A dark character, a womanish character, a stubborn character; bestial, childish, brutish, stupid, fake, coarse and jeering, cheating, tyrannical.

29. If someone who does not know what is in the universe is a stranger to it, someone who does not know what is happening in it is no less a stranger. He is a runaway who flees from the reason that makes us a community. He is blind who shuts the eyes of his understanding. He is poor who needs someone else, and does not have within himself everything that is useful for life. He is an abscess on the universe who, because he is displeased with what happens, withdraws and cuts himself off from the reason of our common nature—for the same nature that brings this about brought you about too. He is a piece torn off from the state who tears his own soul away from the soul of rational beings, which is one.

30. One is a philosopher without a tunic, another without a book; here is another, half-naked. "I have no bread," he says, "and I hold fast to reason"—and I get no living from my learning, and I hold fast to my reason.

31. Love the art you have learned, however humble it may be, and be content with it. And go through the rest of your life as someone who has entrusted everything he has to the gods with his whole soul, making yourself neither a tyrant nor a slave to anyone.

32. Think, for example, of the times of Vespasian. You will see all the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling sick, dying, waging war, feasting, trading, farming the land, flattering, being stubbornly arrogant, suspecting, plotting, wishing for some to die, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for the consulship, for royal power. Well, that life of theirs no longer exists anywhere. Move on again to the times of Trajan. Again, everything is the same. Their life too is gone. Look in the same way at the other periods of time and of whole nations, and see how many, after great efforts, soon fell and were broken up into the elements. But above all, think of the people you yourself have known who wore themselves out over empty things, and neglected to do what was in keeping with their own makeup, and to hold fast to it and be content with it. And here you must remember that the attention given to each thing has its own proper value and proportion. For then you will not lose heart, as long as you give smaller matters no more attention than is fitting.

33. Words that were once in common use are now out of date. So too the names of those who were once famous are now, in a way, out of date: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus; and a little later Scipio and Cato too; then Augustus; then Hadrianus and Antoninus as well. For all things soon fade and become a mere story, and complete oblivion soon buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way. As for the rest, as soon as they have breathed their last they are gone, and no one speaks of them. And, to sum up, what is even everlasting remembrance? Nothing at all. What, then, should we give our serious effort to? This one thing: just thoughts, acts that serve the community, words that never lie, and a disposition that gladly accepts everything that happens as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from a source and origin of the same kind.
34. Give yourself up willingly to Clotho, one of the Fates, and let her spin your thread into whatever she pleases.
35. Everything lasts only a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

36. Watch constantly how all things come about through change, and train yourself to see that the nature of the universe loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will be. But you think only of seeds that are sown in the earth or in a womb; and that is a very crude idea.

37. You will soon die, and you are not yet simple, not yet free from disturbance, not yet free from the suspicion that things outside you can harm you, not yet kind to everyone; nor do you yet place wisdom in acting justly and in that alone.
38. Look into people's ruling faculties, even those of the wise, and see what sort of things they avoid and what sort of things they pursue.

39. What is bad for you does not lie in someone else's ruling faculty, nor in any turn or change of the body that covers you. Where is it, then? It lies in that part of you which has the power to form opinions about what is bad. So let that power not form such opinions, and all is well. And even if the thing nearest to it, your poor body, is cut, burned, full of pus and rot, still let the part that forms opinions about these things stay quiet. That is, let it judge that nothing that can happen equally to a bad person and a good one is either bad or good. For what happens equally to someone who lives against nature and to someone who lives in keeping with nature is neither in keeping with nature nor against it.

40. Always think of the universe as one living being, with one substance and one soul. Notice how everything is referred to one perception, the perception of this one living being; how everything acts by one impulse; and how all things work together as causes of everything that exists. Notice, too, how the thread is spun without a break, and how the web is woven together.
41. You are a little soul carrying a corpse around, as Epictetus used to say.
42. It is nothing bad for things to undergo change, and nothing good for things to exist as a result of change.
43. Time is like a river made of the things that happen, and a violent current. As soon as each thing has been seen, it is swept away, and another comes in its place, and that too will be swept away.

44. Everything that happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and fruit in summer. So it is with disease, death, slander, treachery, and whatever else delights fools or troubles them.

45. In the chain of things, what comes after always fits what went before. For this chain is not like a mere list of unconnected things, joined only because one must follow another; it is a rational connection. And just as all existing things are arranged together in harmony, so the things that come into being show not mere succession, but a wonderful kinship.

46. Always remember what Heraclitus said: that the death of earth is to become water, the death of water is to become air, the death of air is to become fire, and so back again. Think too of the man who forgets where the road leads. Think too how people quarrel with the very thing they are most constantly in touch with, the reason that governs the universe; and that the things they meet every day seem strange to them. And consider that we ought not to act and speak as if we were asleep, for even in sleep we seem to act and speak; and that we ought not, like children taught by their parents, simply to act and speak as we have been taught.

47. If some god told you that you would die tomorrow, or at the latest the day after, you would not much care whether it was the day after or tomorrow—unless you were utterly small-minded. For how small the difference is! In the same way, think it no great thing to die after as many years as you can name rather than tomorrow.

48. Think constantly of how many doctors have died after frowning so often over the sick; how many astrologers, after grandly predicting other people's deaths; how many philosophers, after endless discussions about death or immortality; how many heroes, after killing thousands; how many tyrants, after using their power over people's lives with terrible arrogance, as if they themselves were immortal; and how many whole cities have, so to speak, died—Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others. Add to the count all the people you yourself have known, one after another. One man buried another and was then laid out dead himself, and someone else buried him—and all this in a short time. In short, always see how short-lived and worthless human things are: what was yesterday a little mucus will tomorrow be a mummy or ashes. So pass through this little stretch of time in keeping with nature, and end your journey content, as an olive falls when it is ripe, blessing nature, who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.

49. Be like the headland that the waves keep breaking against: it stands firm, and tames the raging water around it. "Am I unhappy because this has happened to me?" Not at all. Rather: "I am happy, even though this has happened to me, because I remain free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor afraid of the future." For something like this could have happened to anyone; but not everyone would have remained free from pain when it did. Why, then, call that a misfortune rather than this a good fortune? Do you really call something a person's misfortune when it is not a departure from human nature? And does something seem to you a departure from human nature when it is not against what human nature wills? Well, you know what nature wills. Will what has happened, then, stop you from being just, great-souled, self-controlled, sensible, guarded against rash opinions and falsehood? Will it stop you from having modesty, freedom and all the rest—the qualities whose presence gives human nature everything that is its own? Remember too, whenever something leads you toward resentment, to apply this principle: not "this is a misfortune," but "to bear this nobly is good fortune."

50. It is an ordinary kind of help, but still a useful one, toward thinking little of death, to call to mind people who clung hard to life. What more did they gain than those who died early? In the end, surely, they lie in their graves somewhere—Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or anyone else like them, who carried many others out to burial and then were carried out themselves. Altogether, the span between birth and death is small; and think with how much trouble, in the company of what sort of people, and in how feeble a body it is laboriously lived through. So do not regard life as a thing of any value. For look at the vast stretch of time behind you, and at the time ahead of you, another boundless expanse. In this infinity, what difference is there between one who lives three days and one who lives three generations?

51. Always take the short road; and the short road is the natural one. So say and do everything in keeping with the soundest reason. For a purpose like this frees a person from trouble and strife, and from all scheming and showy display.
